In Japanese poetry, the plum blossom (*ume*) is the harbinger of spring, often blooming while the air is still cold. This haiku captures the essence of *fūryū* (refined elegance). It celebrates the luxury of wasting time in the pursuit of beauty. The poet is so enchanted by the "far and near" of the blossoms that he loses track of time, his feet leading him back to the same paths day after day.

Fifty(-year-old) bridegroom;

### 2. Interpretation

The poem depicts a wedding ceremony involving an older man (the "fifty-year-old groom"). In the Edo period, fifty was considered quite old to be a first-time groom, or perhaps he is remarrying. 

The "pate" (*atama* or *tenshō*) refers specifically to the top of the head. In the formal attire of the era, men wore their hair in a topknot (*chonmage*), but age has caused this groom’s hair to thin or disappear. During the formal greetings of the wedding, the groom is using his folding fan—a standard accessory for formal wear—not to cool himself, but as a shield to hide his baldness from the guests or his new bride.

#### A. The "Issa Style" (Haibun-teki)
Issa is known for *haikai* that focuses on the "small" things: insects, poverty, and the awkwardness of human life. Unlike Bashō, who often sought the sublime, or Buson, who sought the aesthetic, Issa looks at the **humorous pathetic**. There is a deep sense of *okashimi* (ridiculousness/wit) here.
